title: Freedom (CCC 1730–1733)
hook: true freedom grows the more we choose the good

segments.voice: Yesterday, sanctifying grace: God's own life, given as a gift. Your line was free, not earned. Today, another kind of free: what people do with their own choices.

Sit someone who has never touched a piano in front of one. Are they free to play anything? In one sense, yes: nobody's stopping them, and they can press any key they like. But they can't play a single song. Now seat a pianist who has practiced every day for twenty years. Same keys, and she's free to play almost anything: Bach, jazz, a song she makes up on the spot. Which of them is freer? The Catholic Church says the pianist, and builds a whole idea of freedom on that answer.
screen: `A BEGINNER AT THE PIANO.` → `A PIANIST OF TWENTY YEARS.` → `WHICH ONE IS FREER?`

segments.voice: It starts with a gift. The Catechism opens with a line from the book of Sirach, which Catholics count as Scripture, in the Douay-Rheims: "God made man from the beginning, and left him in the hand of his own counsel." God doesn't make puppets. He makes people who can say yes or no, even to him. The Catechism describes freedom as a power, rooted in reason and will, to act or not to act, to do this or that, and so to shape your own life. People are responsible for what they freely choose. Here's the surprise: the more a person does what is good, the freer they become. Like the pianist, every good choice is practice, and practice opens up what you're able to do. A Dominican teacher named Servais Pinckaers called it freedom for excellence, next to the thinner idea of freedom as just picking between options. It runs the other way too. Jesus says in John's Gospel: "whosoever committeth sin, is the servant of sin." The Catechism calls choosing evil an abuse of freedom that leads to slavery. Watch a habit take over, the phone late at night, the drink, the lie that needs another lie, and the pattern shows: the more it's done, the less it's chosen. The same chapter holds the promise: "the truth shall make you free." Catholics don't see freedom and goodness as rivals. Goodness is what freedom is for.
screen: `LEFT IN THE HAND OF HIS OWN COUNSEL.` · `THE POWER TO ACT, OR NOT.` · `EVERY GOOD CHOICE IS PRACTICE.` · `SIN MAKES A SERVANT.` · then, large: `THE TRUTH SHALL MAKE YOU FREE.`

segments.voice: Find one small place in your day where you usually go on autopilot: the second scroll, the sharp reply, the thing you always put off. Picture the moment, then picture choosing differently, on purpose, not because you have to but because you can. If you pray, you can ask for the grace to choose it.
Freedom. In Catholic teaching, not just picking between options, but the power to choose the good, a power that grows the more it's used.
Your line: freedom grows. Just ask the pianist at the keys. That's three hundred nine days now.

howItsDone: Catholics are taught that freedom is a gift for choosing the good, and some practice it through daily examination of conscience and small acts of self-discipline, especially in Lent.

notes: Douay-Rheims Ecclesiasticus 15:14, John 8:32 and 8:34 given from memory; confirm wording.
Sirach is deuterocanonical: Catholics count it as Scripture; many Protestants do not. The script says 'which Catholics count as Scripture'.
Pinckaers's 'freedom for excellence' paraphrased from The Sources of Christian Ethics; the piano illustration is the script's own and is commonly used in this connection.
